_doc: Maps a published leaderboard model string to a catalog model id.
A row is ingested only if it matches an entry here. Unmatched rows stay in the
raw archive and are reported by `npm run ingest`; they are never guessed into place.
The catalog holds ONE record per model family and keeps reasoning effort on the
observation row, so `effort` is "*" almost everywhere: a published string identifies the
family, and whatever effort the source printed is stored on the row. Add an effort-specific
entry only if a maker ever ships two records for one family again.
An alias may carry "file": "<batch>", which scopes it to one archive file and wins over a
global entry for the same string. Use it only when a published model string means different
models in different sources -- see the deepseek-v4-flash entry, where the bare string is the
0731 release on Artificial Analysis and the earlier preview on LiveBench, Epoch and LMArena.
Scoping is the last resort, not the first: a string that means one model everywhere gets one
global entry, and a string nobody can attribute stays unmapped and reported.
Two escape hatches, both deliberately requiring a written reason:
acknowledgedDisagreements - {modelId, benchmark, reason} for a cell where two sources really do
measure different things. Without an entry, a disagreement above
20% fails check:data. It used to be reported and ignored, which is
how a preview release published its scores under the name of the
model that replaced it for a week.
mergedInOneSource         - {file, modelId, reason} for a batch where two published strings
really are one model. Without an entry, one source resolving two
strings into one cell fails: a board publishing two entries is that
board saying they are two models.
Deliberately absent, with reasons, so nobody re-adds them by accident:
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite          - NOT a judgement that it is uninteresting. AA measures it and its
parameters are archived, so a record is writable today - but only
three benchmarks carry it (arena-text, critpt, gdpval), one of which
is Arena Elo and never enters a capability table. A record would draw
an empty row across 68 columns. Revisit when a board that publishes
widely - LiveBench, Epoch - carries it; the rows are already being
collected daily and will attach the moment an alias exists.
Claude Sonnet 5 (Non-reasoning, High Effort) - reasoning and non-reasoning are different modes,
but both parse to effort "high", so mapping both put two
operating modes in one cell. Caught by the one-source-one-cell
gate the day it was added. The plain (Non-reasoning) string
carries no effort token and does not collide, so it stays.
Muse Spark (no version)         - a different model from Muse Spark 1.1
GPT-5.5 Pro / 5.2 Pro / 5.4 Pro - Pro is a different model from the base
DeepSeek v4 (max)               - a superseded duplicate, not an ambiguity: this catalog maps
DeepSeek V4 to deepseek-v4-pro, and the row is batch 01's
eye-read 89.6 of batch 12's 89.65. See supersededRows.
GPT 5.6 Sol (Max + Pro)         - a two-model system, not a model configuration
Fable 5 (1M) on PostTrainBench  - the page says failed cells fell back to Opus 4.8
Multiple / Best per task       - leaderboard aggregate rows, not a model at all
MiniMax, Composer, Seed, Qwen3.6, GPT-5.x - not in the catalog yet; archived for later
Opus 4.7/4.6/4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, GLM-5.1, Kimi K2.5, GPT-5.x, Composer 2.5, Seed 2.1 Pro,
Muse Spark (base) - previous generation, or too little operating data to build a record
LiveBench (batch 09) prints lowercase slugs with the effort suffixed onto the model string
(claude-opus-5-max-effort, gpt-5.5-xhigh). The suffix identifies an operating point, not a
separate model, so it maps to the family and the effort stays on the observation row -- the
fetcher copies it into reasoning_effort only when the token literally appears in the string.
LiveBench strings deliberately left unmapped, so nobody adds them by reflex:
gemini-3.5-flash-lite-high      - Flash-Lite is a different model from Flash, not an effort
claude-opus-4-5/4-6/4-7-*       - previous generation, no catalog record
claude-sonnet-4-6-thinking-*    - previous generation, no catalog record
gpt-5.2-*, gpt-5.4-*            - previous generation, no catalog record
qwen3.6-27b                     - the 27B open model, not Qwen3.6 Plus or Max
grok-build-0.1                  - a coding product, not a catalog model
Gemini 3 Flash publishes one line per effort (Minimal/Low/Medium/High) and some sources say
'Preview'. They are the same family as the plain string, which was already mapped for
(Non-reasoning); the effort lives on the observation row. Leaving them unmapped was an
oversight, not a decision -- it stranded the SWE-bench rows in batch 02.
DeepSWE (batch 11) prints dash-separated slugs with no effort in the string (gpt-5-6-sol,
claude-opus-4-8) and publishes one row per effort, so the effort arrives in its own field
and every mapping is "*". gpt-5-4 and claude-sonnet-4-6 are left unmapped: previous
generation, no catalog record.
Epoch AI (batch 12) writes the operating point onto the model string as <slug>_<effort>
(claude-opus-5_max, o1-2024-12-17_low); the fetcher splits it off, so aliases map the bare
slug and the effort rides on the row. Epoch spells families with dots where DeepSWE uses
dashes, hence both gpt-5.6-sol and gpt-5-6-sol appear here. Terminal-Bench (batch 13) uses
the board's display labels instead ("Fable 5", "GLM-5.1").
Left unmapped from these two batches: claude-opus-4-5/4-6/4-7, claude-sonnet-4-6, gpt-5.x and
o-series snapshots, glm-5/5.1, gemini-2.x/3-pro-preview, qwen3.5/3.6-flash, muse-spark (base),
and the _16K/_32K/_120K context variants -- previous generation or no catalog record.

aliases.reason: DeepSeek shipped V4 Flash twice: a preview, then the post-trained 0731 release, whose scores are much higher. LiveBench, Epoch and LMArena publish both and print -0731 for the official one, so the bare string there is the preview and must not reach this record. Artificial Analysis never renamed its slug: the bare string with no effort is 'DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (Reasoning, Max Effort)', published 2026-07-31, per the row's own note. Hence the file scope. AA's non-reasoning row under the same string is the 2026-04-24 preview and stays unmapped.

LiveBench, Epoch and the QwenCloud parameter rows all spell the flagship this way. There is exactly one Qwen3.8 string published anywhere in the archive — no Plus, no Flash, no preview and no dated snapshot — so no size or tier word has to be stripped to reach the family, which is the case the attribution rule warns about.
DeepSWE's spelling: dashes throughout, effort in its own field. Same family as qwen3.8-max above.

Agents' Last Exam, and not the doubled spelling it uses for the 3.7 family (qwen-qwen3-7-max) — the board is inconsistent about the prefix, so the identity was confirmed on the number rather than on the string: ALE publishes 26.97 pass rate with a 52.49 partial score under claude_code, and Qwen's own release table publishes 27 with a 52.4 partial for Qwen3.8-Max. Two readings of the same run, agreeing on both numbers, which no other Qwen string does.

Artificial Analysis' GDPval-AA leaderboard (batch 19), which spells families as display labels with a space. It appeared in the 2026-08-06 refresh — AA's evaluation boards picked this model up before its parameter API did, which is why the catalog record carries a GDPval score and no intelligence index. The other Qwen string in the same batch is 'Qwen3 8B (Reasoning)' at 213 Elo, a different model entirely; this one is 1739.

Qwen's own release table (batch 17) prints the display label. It needs its own entry rather than relying on the lowercase one because alias resolution is case-sensitive — the case check:models fails on. Batch 17's competitor columns stay refused per-file; this is the one column that is Qwen's own model, so it is a vendor reading of the maker's own release and lands in twelve catalog columns, four of which no other source fills.

Batch 17 is Qwen's own release table and it prints a column per competitor. Those numbers are archived as evidence but must not be ingested: a maker publishing a rival's score states no harness, no reasoning effort and no benchmark version, and source precedence puts it below every board that does. Several of these strings resolve globally from other batches, so the refusal has to be scoped to this file rather than expressed by leaving them out.

benchmarkSplits.reason: Tier 4 is a harder, separate problem set from Tiers 1-3. Kept in one cell they would share a table column, so one model's Tier 4 score would be read against another model's Tiers 1-3 score.
Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1 are different task sets and the architecture forbids merging them. 2.0 gets its own legacy-tier benchmark so the 2.1 column stays clean.

versionAliases.reason: ARC Prize writes the version as '2'; the catalog and the existing rows write 'v2'. Same version, different spelling.
Scale calls it the 'Public Dataset'; existing rows call it 'Public'. Same 731-instance public split.
Same verified split, written with and without the benchmark name as a prefix.

Same v2 leaderboard, written with and without the benchmark name as a prefix.
The MMMU-Pro Overall column is what the catalog already records as 'Pro'. The Vision and Standard subsets are deliberately not ingested rather than folded in.
Evidence-backed: Mercor's Pass@1 values match the existing rows exactly for Fable 5 (43.3) and GPT-5.6 Sol (39.9), so '2026' is a placeholder label for the same Pass@1 metric.

JUDGEMENT CALL, not an exact match. Both refer to Scale's MCP-Atlas board, but the values differ by 1-2 points from the existing vendor rows (Kimi K3 84.2 vs 82.3, Fable 5 84.7 vs 83.3). Treated as one version so the column stays single-versioned; the gap is visible as two rows in the cell, benchmark-native first.

droppedBenchmarks.reason: 383 rows of LMArena text Elo. Arena is a human-preference lens, not a capability benchmark, and the catalog already carries textElo/codeElo on the model record. Ingesting it as a benchmark would put preference into the capability tables.

Two to three rows each and tool-dependent definitions; not enough to form a comparable column yet. Archived for later.

Published in the Qwen3.8 release tables (batch 17) and archived there as evidence, but the catalog has no record for these benchmarks. Most are Qwen-authored (QwenSWEBench, QwenReactBench, QwenVisualOffice), vision or video suites the dashboard does not track, or a benchmark whose only reading anywhere is this vendor table -- a column built from one maker's numbers about its own release would rank nothing. Listed in full so the next release is not re-derived from scratch. OSWorld-Verified is here on purpose: it is a different evaluation from OSWorld 2.0, which is carried, and the same table prints 86.1 against 19.4 for one model.

versionFallbacks.reason: Vals AI runs one current version of each of these and publishes no version label. These benchmark records were created for this project, so no other source competes for the column and the label cannot collide. The retrievedDate on each row pins the snapshot. Deliberately NOT applied to SWE-Marathon, PostTrainBench or ProgramBench, where an unlabelled row would land in a column that already holds vendor numbers of unknown provenance.
Vals publishes no version for its swe-verified run. 'Verified' is the name of the evaluation split, not a release number, so recording it asserts nothing beyond what the source states.

supersededRows.reason: Batch 02 transcribed the DeepSWE board by eye: 18 rows of its 'Best view', rounded to whole points (74 where the artifact says 73.6). Batch 11 reads the same page's own artifact and gets all 50 configurations at full precision. These are not two measurements, they are one measurement read twice, so ingesting both would put two rows in one cell and let the rounded one win the primary slot -- a system benchmark keeps the highest score within a source class, and 74 beats 73.6. The rows stay in the archive because they are real evidence of what the page showed on 2026-07-31.

Batch 02 transcribed the Terminal-Bench 2.1 board by eye. Batch 13 reads the Supabase function the page itself calls, which returns the same submissions with the agent, reasoning effort, run date, trial count and pass@k attached. One measurement read twice, so only the scripted reading is ingested. Scoped to version 2.1 deliberately: batch 02 also holds Terminal-Bench 2.0 rows under the same benchmark name, they map to the separate terminal-20 column, and no scripted source replaces them.

256K is the Tinker Serverless Inference product serving limit (the pricing page lists it per product tier), not the model's architectural context window. The architectural maximum (1,048,576 from HF config.json model_max_length) is carried in batch-15. Both values are real published facts and both stay in the archive unchanged; this entry tells the provenance check to use batch-15 for the context_k field, so the catalog's 1000K is backed rather than disputed. Scoped to modelRaw + field so other models in batch-08 are unaffected.

Same as Inkling above: 256K is the Serverless Inference serving limit, not the context window. config.json model_max_length is 1,048,576 (batch-15). Both stay in the archive; this entry routes the provenance check to batch-15 for this field.

Batch 01 transcribed the Epoch GPQA Diamond board by eye: 20 rows with the reasoning effort folded into the model string and scores rounded to one decimal. Batch 12 reads Epoch's own hub export and gets the same board at full precision with effort in its own field. One measurement read twice, so only the scripted reading is ingested -- gpt-5.5 (xhigh) 94.0 is batch 12's 94, GPT-5.5 Pro (xhigh) 93.9 is 93.92, GPT-5.5 (low) 90.7 is 90.66, and DeepSeek v4 (max) 89.6 is deepseek-v4-pro's 89.65. Comparing the two batches by model string understates the overlap, because only batch 01 writes the effort into the name; the correspondence is by model plus effort. The rows stay in the archive unchanged.

Batch 03 hand-read the ALE board on the stated grounds that it publishes nothing machine-readable. It does: the leaderboard page calls /api/demo/leaderboard, which returns every run with pass rate, partial credit, task counts and cost. One measurement read twice -- the endpoint gives GPT-5.6 Sol under Codex a passRate of 0.30592 where the transcription recorded 30.6, and an avgScore of 0.53616 where the note recorded 53.6% -- so ingesting both would put a rounded row and an exact row in one cell. The transcribed rows stay in the archive as evidence of what the page showed on 2026-07-31.

Batch 16 hand-read three ALE rows to patch what batch 03 missed. Batch 18 reads the endpoint and carries 57 configurations across 24 models, including all three. Superseded for the same reason as batch 03: same measurement, more digits.

Batch 04 hand-read 14 rows off the GDPval-AA board. Batch 19 renders the same page and reads all 175 configurations, and it re-reads the harness and tool setting from the page text every run instead of carrying the transcriptions assumption forward. One measurement read twice; the transcribed rows stay in the archive as evidence of what the board showed on 2026-07-31.

Batch 04 hand-read two rows off the MMMU board. Batch 20 reads all 71 that carry an MMMU-Pro Overall score, and reads the one thing the transcription got wrong: the board's legend says '*: results provided by the authors', so a starred score is a vendor self-report. Both transcribed rows recorded 'Author-reported result' in their note and were filed as source_kind benchmark anyway — the highest precedence this project has — so a self-report was outranking every verified reading in its cell. The transcribed rows also carry benchmark_version 'MMMU-Pro · Overall' where the column is 'Pro', which would put two versions in one cell.
